Measuring Redshift from DESI Spectra, Without Redrock¶

What this is. A record of learning to determine spectroscopic redshift from flux and inverse-variance alone, and — just as important — learning to tell when the answer cannot be determined and should be refused.

Constraint. The inputs are BRZ_FLUX and BRZ_IVAR, plus imaging-derived metadata (TARGET_CLASS / DESI_TARGET, TSNR2_*) which exists before any spectrum is taken. No Redrock code, templates, or derived products were used. The catalogue redshift Z is Redrock's answer and is used only for scoring and as one vote in a three-way consistency check — never inside the pipeline. Every module in the measurement path was checked to contain no reference to Z, SPECTYPE, or CHI2.

Headline.

dataset spectra agreement (all) answered accuracy on answered tier-1
val_80k (sv3) 20,000 97.60% 94.8% 99.26% 72.0% @ 99.70%
p100 (main) 10,000 93.23% 93.7% 97.37% 74.4% @ 98.79%
p080 (main) 10,000 90.54% 87.7% 97.55% 60.6% @ 99.21%
p020 (main) 10,000 89.59% 86.5% 97.20% 57.4% @ 99.20%
p000 (main) 10,000 48.83% 63.5% 68.44% 29.8% @ 64.45%

The two datasets are not measuring the same thing — see the Provenance section. That caveat is part of the result.

Two numbers here need their caveat stated immediately. p000's accuracy falls under the final pipeline, from 71.38% to 68.44%. That is not a regression: the pipeline now confidently identifies p000's stellar targets as stars, and is scored against a catalogue that places 52% of them at z≈1.68. Section 22 shows the two figures agreeing to one decimal place. And earlier drafts of this report quoted p080 at 82.9% answered — a figure that predates a threshold change in decide.py; the correct like-for-like baseline is 86.2%.

Part II (sections 18–23) removes the imaging class entirely and asks whether the object type can be read from the spectrum itself. It can — and doing so exposed a defect in the confidence measure worth +642 answers with zero losses on the independent survey.

import os, sys, warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.expanduser('~/claude_learning_map'))
import numpy as np, h5py
import matplotlib
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams['figure.dpi'] = 110
plt.rcParams['font.size'] = 9

BASE = '/pscratch/sd/s/shunth/claude_learning_map'
LEVELS = ['p100', 'p080', 'p060', 'p040', 'p020', 'p000']
CN = ['BGS', 'LRG', 'ELG', 'QSO', 'STAR']
TOL = 0.003          # |dz|/(1+z) < 0.003, the standard catastrophic-failure mark

import decide as DEC

def load(lv):
    d = dict(np.load(f'{BASE}/prod_{lv}.npz', allow_pickle=True))
    ok = np.abs((d['z'] - d['zA']) / (1 + d['zA'])) < TOL
    # the stored tier predates a threshold change in decide.py; recompute it
    # from the stored significance so these tables reproduce from the code as
    # it now stands rather than from whatever it was on the day
    d['tier'], d['reason'] = DEC.verdict(d['sig'], d['tclass'], d['z'])
    return d, ok

P = {lv: load(lv) for lv in LEVELS}
V = np.load(f'{BASE}/prod_val80k.npz', allow_pickle=True)
Vok = np.abs((V['z'] - V['zA']) / (1 + V['zA'])) < TOL
print('loaded', {lv: len(P[lv][1]) for lv in LEVELS}, ' val_80k:', len(Vok))

1. The one structural fact everything is built on¶

A redshift is a pure translation in ln(lambda):

$$\lambda_{\rm obs} = \lambda_{\rm rest}(1+z) \;\Longrightarrow\; \ln\lambda_{\rm obs} = \ln\lambda_{\rm rest} + \ln(1+z)$$

So on a uniform ln-lambda grid, scanning every redshift is one cross-correlation, computable for all z at once by FFT. With inverse-variance weights the best-fit amplitude has a closed form, and

$$\Delta\chi^2(z) = \frac{A(z)^2}{B(z)},\qquad A=\textstyle\sum w f T_z,\quad B=\textstyle\sum w T_z^2$$

where both $A$ and $B$ are themselves correlations. 13,101 redshifts cost two forward FFTs and a handful of inverse ones.

2. First, verify the wavelength convention¶

Air vs vacuum is an 80 km/s systematic — enough to destroy the precision budget. Rather than assume, measure it: stack continuum-subtracted galaxies around a line at its vacuum and air wavelengths and see which centres on zero velocity.

In [2]:
from scipy.ndimage import median_filter
H5V = f'{BASE}/val_80k.h5'
wave = 3600.0 + 0.8*np.arange(7781)
with h5py.File(H5V,'r') as f:
    zt = f['Z'][:4000]
    sp = np.array([s.decode() for s in f['SPECTYPE'][:4000]])
    sel = np.where((sp=='GALAXY') & (zt>0.05) & (zt<0.45))[0][:350]
    fl = f['BRZ_FLUX'][sel]; iv = f['BRZ_IVAR'][sel]
zs = zt[sel]

def stack(restw):
    v = np.linspace(-400, 400, 161); out=[]
    for i in range(len(sel)):
        lo = restw*(1+zs[i])
        if lo < 3700 or lo > 9700: continue
        c = median_filter(fl[i].astype(float), 201)
        r = (fl[i]-c)*np.sqrt(np.maximum(iv[i],0))
        out.append(np.interp(lo*(1+v/299792.458), wave, r))
    return v, np.median(out,0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11,3.4))
for a,(nm, vac, air) in zip(ax, [('[O III] 5008', 5008.240, 5006.84),
                                 ('H-alpha', 6564.61, 6562.80)]):
    v, sv = stack(vac); _, sa = stack(air)
    a.plot(v, sv, label=f'vacuum {vac}', lw=1.6)
    a.plot(v, sa, label=f'air {air}', lw=1.2, ls='--')
    a.axvline(0, color='0.6', lw=0.8)
    a.set_title(f'{nm}: peak at vacuum {v[np.argmax(sv)]:+.0f} km/s, '
                f'air {v[np.argmax(sa)]:+.0f} km/s', fontsize=8)
    a.set_xlabel('velocity offset (km/s)'); a.legend(fontsize=7)
ax[0].set_ylabel('stacked significance')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print('DESI wavelengths are VACUUM. Using air values would introduce ~+80 km/s.')

DESI wavelengths are VACUUM. Using air values would introduce ~+80 km/s.

Result: the vacuum wavelength centres on 0 km/s; the air value is displaced by ~80 km/s. Every line list in this work is vacuum.

3. Different classes carry redshift in different physics¶

This was the single most important conceptual correction. I began assuming one universal method; roughly half the objects do not carry their redshift in emission lines at all.

class what actually carries the redshift consequence
ELG the resolved [O II] 3727/3729 doublet needs lines; nothing else works
LRG / BGS the 4000 A break + Ca II H&K a continuum feature, not a line
STAR z ~ 0 a classification problem, not a measurement
QSO broad UV lines + the Lyman-alpha forest edge again a break above z~2

The measurement below makes the point quantitatively: at the same redshift and with the same lines available, BGS and QSO have nearly identical line strength but wildly different accuracy — because when the lines fade BGS still has a continuum to stand on and a quasar does not.

In [3]:

      f'{"sig|agree":>11s}{"sig|disagree":>14s}')
for r in rows:

print('\nBGS and QSO have the same line strength (9.64 vs 9.46) and differ by')
print('45 points of accuracy. The difference is the continuum fallback.')

4. Architecture¶

Three stages. The separation matters and was learned the hard way.

Stage 1 — candidate generation. High-passed matched filters, every model scanned over all redshifts by FFT. Recall is what matters here; precision does not. Each model gets a guaranteed quota of peaks.

Stage 2 — decision. Every candidate refitted against one common, unfiltered data vector, each model given the same Legendre nuisance terms.

Stage 3 — verdict. Answer, flag, or decline.

Two rules that cost me a great deal to learn:

  1. chi2 from differently-filtered data is not comparable. Models with wider high-pass retain more variance and win spuriously. I fixed this at the decision stage early, then left the identical bug in candidate ranking for a long time (see section 8).
  2. Where a learned basis has no training coverage it must contribute zero WEIGHT, never a prediction of zero flux. Otherwise every redshift that shifts real data into the uncovered region is punished, dragging answers to low z.

5. Results across the SNR ladder¶

These are the numbers at the end of Part I — the pipeline as built from imaging-conditioned templates and the two decline rules. Part II (sections 18-23) removes the imaging class, finds a defect in the confidence measure, and improves on every row of this table; the comparison is in section 21.

The tier is recomputed here from the stored significance rather than read from the saved run, so the table reproduces from the current code.

Note that p080 through p020 behave almost identically. That is not a coincidence — their median SNR_PROXY values are 11.9 / 11.4 / 11.0 / 10.5, i.e. they are effectively one regime, while p100 (23.9) and p000 (3.0) sit outside it. The difficulty ladder is not evenly spaced.

6. The confidence measure: feature significance at my own answer¶

Everything I tried first was indirect — a chi2 margin, a posterior mass, whether a second method happened to agree. The measure that works is direct: the matched-filter significance of the class's defining feature, evaluated at the redshift I just predicted. It requires no truth.

In [6]:
S = np.load(f'{BASE}/selfconf.npz', allow_pickle=True)
bins = [(0,3),(3,5),(5,10),(10,20),(20,1e9)]
lab  = ['<3','3-5','5-10','10-20','>20']
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11,3.6))
for lv in ['p100','p060','p020','p000']:
    sig = S[f'{lv}_sig']; zc = S[f'{lv}_zC']; zA = S[f'{lv}_zA']
    ok = np.abs((zc-zA)/(1+zA)) < TOL
    y = [ok[(sig>=a)&(sig<b)].mean()*100 if ((sig>=a)&(sig<b)).sum()>15
         else np.nan for a,b in bins]
    ax[0].plot(range(len(bins)), y, 'o-', label=lv, ms=5)
ax[0].set_xticks(range(len(bins))); ax[0].set_xticklabels(lab)
ax[0].set_xlabel('feature significance at my own answer (sigma)')
ax[0].set_ylabel('% correct'); ax[0].legend(fontsize=7); ax[0].grid(alpha=.3)
ax[0].set_title('monotonic and stable across an 8x SNR range')

d,ok = P['p040']
for t,c,l in [(1,'tab:green','tier 1'),(2,'tab:orange','tier 2'),(3,'tab:red','tier 3')]:
    ax[1].hist(np.clip(d['sig'][d['tier']==t],-2,40), bins=60, alpha=.6,
               color=c, label=l)
ax[1].set_xlabel('feature significance'); ax[1].set_ylabel('count')
ax[1].legend(fontsize=7); ax[1].set_title('p040: what the tiers separate on')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Calibration is the point. >10 sigma is ~99% correct at every depth; <3 sigma is ~17%. That is a usable, physically interpretable confidence: "I can see the lines at N sigma."

Thresholds differ per class because BGS, LRG and STAR are continuum-driven — asking them for a line detection declines objects that are perfectly well measured. Getting this wrong was costing real accuracy (section 8).

7. The second decline rule: the default exit¶

A featureless spectrum has nowhere to go. The stellar template is the only one that needs no lines at all — it can always fit a continuum shape — so that is where a fit lands when there is no information. For a target that imaging says is a galaxy, that answer is nearly always wrong, and it is detectable without truth.

In [7]:
rec=[]
for lv in LEVELS:
    d, ok = P[lv]
    z, cls = d['z'], d['tclass']
    z0 = (cls!='STAR') & (np.abs(z)<0.01)
    bad = ~ok
    rec.append(dict(level=lv,
                    frac_z0=z0.mean()*100,
                    share_of_failures=(z0&bad).sum()/max(bad.sum(),1)*100,
                    correct_when_z0=ok[z0].mean()*100 if z0.sum() else np.nan))
display(pd.DataFrame(rec).set_index('level').round(2))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5,3.4))
x=np.arange(len(LEVELS))
ax.bar(x-0.2,[r['share_of_failures'] for r in rec],0.4,label='% of failures that are z~0')
ax.bar(x+0.2,[r['correct_when_z0'] for r in rec],0.4,label='% correct when I say z~0')
ax.set_xticks(x); ax.set_xticklabels(LEVELS); ax.legend(fontsize=7); ax.grid(alpha=.3)
ax.set_title('the "no information -> z~0" failure mode'); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

8. Quasars: the remaining error is mostly physical, not algorithmic¶

Relaxing the pass mark recovers quasars and nothing else.

In [8]:
tols=[0.003,0.006,0.010,0.020]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6,3.6))
d, ok = P['p100']; keep = d['tier']<3
for c in CN:
    k=(d['tclass']==c)&keep
    ax.plot(tols, [ (np.abs((d['z'][k]-d['zA'][k])/(1+d['zA'][k]))<t).mean()*100
                    for t in tols], 'o-', label=c, ms=5)
ax.set_xscale('log'); ax.set_xlabel('tolerance |dz|/(1+z)'); ax.set_ylabel('% agree')
ax.legend(fontsize=7); ax.grid(alpha=.3)
ax.set_title('p100 answered set: only QSO moves')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print('QSO 90.6 -> 95.8 -> 97.9;  every galaxy class is flat.')

QSO 90.6 -> 95.8 -> 97.9;  every galaxy class is flat.

Why. Broad quasar lines do not sit at the systemic velocity. Measured independently here against the catalogue (~6000 quasars):

line offset (km/s) NMAD within 300 km/s
H-beta −13 108 95.7%
[O III] 5008 −38 119 92.7%
Mg II −73 384 54.8%
C IV −469 624 28.3%
C III] −988 664 8.9%
Ly-alpha +968 947 14.9%

C IV and C III] are blueshifted by the outflowing wind. Ly-alpha is redshifted because the forest eats its blue wing — and the effect grows with redshift (+1008 km/s at z~2.5, +1711 at z>3), exactly as an increasingly opaque forest predicts.

Above z~2 the best available tracer scatters by 500–600 km/s while the pass mark is 900 km/s. The tolerance is only 1.5–2.7x the intrinsic ambiguity of what a quasar's redshift even means.

Attempting to correct this made things worse (−3.9 points): single-line centroids are less precise than the full template fit even after debiasing. A debiased noisy estimator is still noisy.

9. Cross-dataset validation¶

Everything above was developed on the main-survey SNR files. val_80k is a different survey (sv3), a different target selection, and 80,000 spectra. Nothing was tuned on it — the decline thresholds were even updated while this job sat in the queue, so it ran as a blind test of them.

10. Provenance: these two numbers do not measure the same thing¶

val_80k scores higher than p100 (97.63% vs 93.23%). It is tempting to read that as the method doing better on sv3. It is not.

In [10]:
with h5py.File(H5V,'r') as f:
    print('val_80k CATALOG_FILTER:'); print('   ', f.attrs['CATALOG_FILTER'])
print("\nZWARN != 0 among the 80,000:", int((V['zwarn']!=0).sum()))
print("\nThe main-survey SNR files apply only COADD_FIBERSTATUS == 0 -- no ZWARN cut.")
print("So val_80k is agreement with a catalogue that already removed the")
print("redshifts IT considered unreliable; the SNR files are not.")

val_80k CATALOG_FILTER:
    SURVEY == "sv3" and ZCAT_PRIMARY == True and OBJTYPE == "TGT" and ZWARN == 0

ZWARN != 0 among the 80,000: 0

The main-survey SNR files apply only COADD_FIBERSTATUS == 0 -- no ZWARN cut.
So val_80k is agreement with a catalogue that already removed the
redshifts IT considered unreliable; the SNR files are not.

This also means my intended check — does my decline agree with the catalogue's own reliability flag? — is unanswerable on this file by construction, since every object has ZWARN == 0.

I read this filter in my very first command and then stopped carrying it forward once I moved to the new files, and nearly reported the two numbers side by side as if comparable. The failure mode has a name worth remembering: provenance decays. A quantity keeps its label while its meaning changes underneath. The correction is to re-read how each dataset was selected at the moment of comparison, not once at the start.

11. What the spectra actually look like¶

Two objects from p040: one the pipeline answers with high confidence, one it declines. Plotted as noise-normalised residual, so a real line is a genuine excursion above the +/-2 sigma grass.

                 f'my feature significance = {d["sig"][r]:.1f} sigma',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

The declined one is not a case of choosing the wrong redshift — there is no line at the catalogue redshift either. Verified on the full sample rather than from a handful of pictures:

level group n sig at catalogue z sig at my z
p040 ELG correct 600 10.83 10.83
p040 ELG failed 363 1.14 1.14
p020 ELG failed 381 1.11 1.21
p000 ELG failed 600 1.38 1.51

Both hypotheses are unsupported. That is an information limit, not an algorithmic one, and the correct action is to decline.

12. What failed — the honest tally¶

This matters more than the successes, because the pattern is so consistent.

Worked (3) — every one a bug fix, every one found by looking at spectra:

fix gain
uncovered basis region → zero weight, not zero flux large; removed a systematic pull to low z
candidate shortlist ranked incomparable chi2 across models → per-model quota LRG +3.4 / +4.8
high-pass narrower than the feature it must preserve weak-line significance 3.3 → 13.1

Failed (11) — every one added physics, a bigger model, or more data:

attempt result
[O III] 2.98 exact ratio constraint weight 0
imaging redshift priors +0.05
dedicated [O II]-doublet proposer +0.01
Ly-alpha forest consistency rescoring negative
bigger, z-stratified ELG/QSO templates −0.4 / −0.7
per-line velocity debiasing (all lines) −3.9
narrow-line-only refinement −0.3
BPT-selected narrow-line AGN template population is 134 objects; +0.06
splitting QSO into two redshift regimes −0.4
favouring galaxy templates for low-z quasars −5
image-first routing (any threshold) −4.8 vs formula-first

The lesson. A learned PCA template already encodes the physics I was about to hand-write. Hand-crafted constraints help only where learning has too little data to find them itself. The remaining errors were never a missing formula.

13. Image-first or formula-first? Settled by experiment¶

Both readouts were given the identical evidence — a (2048 redshift x 32 feature) significance map — so the comparison is about how evidence is read, not who got better inputs.

path p100 p020
hand-written Bayesian formula on the map 46.0 42.5
CNN on the same map 89.5 83.7
formula proposes → CNN picks 64.4 58.5
CNN proposes → formula picks 61.6 56.3
full-spectrum template fit 93.2 89.4

Three conclusions:

  1. Given the same evidence, a learned readout beats my hand-written formula decisively (89.5 vs 46.0).
  2. Neither ordering helps. Both hybrids are worse than the better method alone, because gating a strong decider behind a weak proposer caps it at the proposer's recall.
  3. Representation dominates readout. The full-spectrum formula beats the CNN on the compressed map. Compressing a spectrum into a 32-column image costs ~5 points that no readout recovers.

The complementarity is tiny and one-sided: the image is right where the formula is wrong only 1.2–1.4% of the time, while the reverse is 6–9%.

So: formulas for production, images for diagnosis. Which is exactly how the three bug fixes above were found.

14. What I learned¶

Information is what constrains wrong answers, not what confirms right ones. Measured three ways: narrow-window group formulas score 41–49% where the full-spectrum template scores 88–93%; the same formula reaches 99.9% on STARs purely because their search range is tiny; the compressed-map CNN loses to the full spectrum. With 2048 trial redshifts, suppressing false alarms is the problem, and that is done by the flux between the lines.

Classes fail at different stages, and the bottleneck moves. ELG loses to candidate generation, QSO to the decision — so effort spent tuning ELG scoring was doomed before it started. At low SNR the QSO bottleneck migrates to candidates too. Diagnose the stage before choosing the fix.

Whether hard data helps depends on label purity, not on SNR. The identical easy→hard curriculum hurt when labels came from weak self-training and helped (+3.9 at the hard end) when they came from a three-way consensus.

Splitting a model is not free. It costs statistical power and adds a selection decision; both exceeded the specialisation gain at this sample size.

The biggest single win was refusal, not accuracy. No modelling change came close to what "know when not to answer" delivered — +4 points at p100, +29 at p000.

Two reasoning errors I made repeatedly, and the guards against them:

  • Small-sample generalisation. Twice a mechanism inferred from ~6 rendered spectra evaporated on the full sample (a "systematic +1500 km/s quasar bias" was really −17.5, and debiasing gained 0.00). Guard: form the hypothesis from pictures, always verify on everything before changing code.
  • Selection effects. "This model is 85.8% pure when it wins" is not "it would be 85.8% if it won more" — it wins because it fits. My +12-point estimate delivered +0.5. Guard: for any number computed on a subset, ask first how that subset was chosen.

And a physical instinct that proved wrong. Measuring the instrument LSF (0.8–1.0 px) suggested my 2.25 px filter was far too wide. The data said the opposite: real ELG lines peak at 3.2–4.5 px, because galaxy kinematics and the [O II] doublet splitting dominate the instrument. Following the "rigorous" derivation would have cost 20% of signal. Any parameter derived from physics still has to be measured.

15. Where the remaining error is¶

At p100, per class, on what the pipeline answers:

  • BGS 99.0%, LRG 98.5%, ELG 99.1%, STAR 99.95% — at the measurement floor
  • QSO 90.6%, of which ~7.3 points are the tolerance sitting inside the physical ambiguity of a quasar redshift; ~1.7% are genuinely catastrophic

The declined 6.8% has ~1.1–1.5 sigma of feature strength at both the catalogue redshift and mine — three independent measurements agree there is nothing to find.

16. The last open question, and how it resolved¶

Low-redshift quasar targets were the worst-performing group (z<1: 67.8%). I proposed they were narrow-line AGN (Seyfert 2) and that the template library lacked that shape. Two measurements disproved it.

First, the BPT diagnostic. The standard separator between AGN-photoionised and star-formation-photoionised gas is log([O III]/Hb) against log([N II]/Ha) with the Kewley (2001) maximum-starburst line. I was already measuring all four lines — but for their significance, never their ratio. Significance says whether a line is there; the ratio says what lit it up.

So the target class was the wrong unit. What decides whether an object can be measured is not what imaging called it, but whether it has a continuum feature to fall back on when its lines are too faint:

  • BGS at this redshift: D4000 = 1.48 — the break alone fixes the redshift, so it reaches 98.5% even though its lines are weak (H-alpha EW 2.9)
  • ELG and QSO targets: D4000 ~ 1.04 — no break, so faint lines leave nothing

That is the same "no continuum fallback" mechanism already established for quasars, but it turns out to describe a population — blue, break-less, high-equivalent-width objects — that cuts across target classes.

The correction that matters: there is no missing template. I twice proposed one (narrow-line AGN, then a low-z ELG specialist) and both gained nothing, because the objects are not a distinct spectral shape — they are ordinary emission-line galaxies whose lines happen to be too faint, with no continuum to fall back on. High equivalent width misled me: EW is a ratio, so a faint object on a faint continuum has high EW and low signal-to-noise. Equivalent width is not detectability.

What remains genuinely unknown is narrower than I thought: not "what are these objects" but "is there any information left in a blue, break-less spectrum whose lines sit below ~3 sigma" — and the evidence so far says no.

17. The class I skipped, and what it revealed¶

I studied ELG, LRG and QSO with rendered spectra. STAR I never looked at, because at 99%+ it seemed solved — and BGS only ever appeared as a control. STAR is 20% of every level and collapses to 47.5% at p000, which I had never examined.

Two failure modes, both instructive.

At mid depth (~1% of stars): unmistakable A-type stars — deep Balmer series, declining red continuum — assigned z = 2.997. A stellar Balmer decrement converging on 3646 A and a Lyman-forest break are both "much absorption in the blue", and the templates are degenerate against each other.

At p000: smooth, featureless, monotonically rising red continua, to which the catalogue assigns z = 1.68065 and z = 1.68124 — nearly identical values for two different objects. That is the signature of a template defaulting, and it turned out not to be rare.

About a third of the apparent p000 stellar failure is the reference, not the method.

The claim has to be stated carefully. This demonstrates the reference is untrustworthy on those objects; it does not prove my answer is right on them. But a score computed against a defaulting template carries no information in either direction. The honest treatment of p000 is to report it with the pile-up excluded, or not to report accuracy there at all.

Why this matters beyond p000. Everything in this report is "agreement with the catalogue". I checked the selection of each dataset (section 10) but had been treating the catalogue values as uniformly reliable. They are not, and the place they fail is exactly the place I was working hardest.

And it was found in the one class I had skipped — because it looked easy. Solved-looking classes are where unexamined assumptions survive longest.

Part II — Reading the type off the spectrum¶

Everything above conditions on TARGET_CLASS, which comes from imaging. This part removes it, asks whether the type can be read from the spectrum itself, and follows what that exposes.

18. Blind test: type and redshift from the picture alone¶

Protocol: random spectra, rendered with no class and no catalogue redshift. The type and redshift were written down before the answers were revealed. Two rounds, 16 spectra, at p100 and p060.

Below are four of them, now annotated with the line identifications that were made from the picture, and with the catalogue answer added afterwards.

In [17]:
import newdata as ND
from scipy.ndimage import median_filter, uniform_filter1d

W = 3600.0 + 0.8 * np.arange(7781)

def getspec(lv, row):
    with h5py.File(ND.path(lv), 'r') as f:
        return f['BRZ_FLUX'][row].astype(float), f['BRZ_IVAR'][row].astype(float)

def continuum(fl, iv, w=121):
    good = iv > 0
    num = uniform_filter1d(np.where(good, fl * iv, 0.), w)
    den = uniform_filter1d(np.where(good, iv, 0.), w)
    return np.where(den > 0, num / np.maximum(den, 1e-30), np.nan)

def sigspec(fl, iv, nsm):
    good = iv > 0
    c = np.nan_to_num(continuum(fl, iv, 301))
    res = np.where(good, fl - c, 0.)
    a = uniform_filter1d(res * np.where(good, iv, 0.), nsm) * nsm
    b = np.sqrt(np.maximum(uniform_filter1d(np.where(good, iv, 0.), nsm) * nsm, 1e-30))
    return a / b

# level, row, blind call, truth, lines used, matched filter width in pixels
BLIND = [
    ('p100', 2096, 'QSO, z~3.10', 'QSO target, z=3.10504', 61,
     [('Lya', 1215.67), ('SiIV', 1399.8), ('CIV', 1549.5), ('CIII]', 1908.7)]),
    ('p060', 5509, 'STAR (A/F), z~0', 'QSO target, z=-0.00021', 31,
     [('Hd', 4102.9), ('Hg', 4341.7), ('Hb', 4862.7), ('Ha', 6564.6)]),
    ('p060', 7951, 'ELG, z~0.811', 'ELG target, z=0.81287', 9,
     [('[OII]', 3728.5), ('Hb', 4862.7), ('[OIII]', 5008.2)]),
    ('p100', 1176, 'declined at first', 'BGS target, z=0.09791', 9,
     [('CaK', 3933.7), ('CaH', 3968.5), ('Gband', 4304.), ('Mgb', 5175.)]),
]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 2, figsize=(14, 11))
for (lv, row, mine, truth, nsm, lines), (axL, axR) in zip(BLIND, axes):
    fl, iv = getspec(lv, row)
    zc = np.load(f'{BASE}/blind_{lv}.npz', allow_pickle=True)['zA'][row]
    lam = np.array([l * (1 + zc) for _, l in lines])
    hi_x = min(9400, max(7000, lam.max() * 1.12))

    c = continuum(fl, iv)
    axL.plot(W, c, lw=1.2, color='C0')
    lo, hi = np.nanpercentile(c, [1, 99]); pad = .25 * (hi - lo) + 1e-9
    axL.set_ylim(lo - pad, hi + pad)
    axL.set_title(f'{lv} row {row}  |  read blind as: {mine}  |  truth: {truth}',
                  fontsize=8.5, loc='left')
    axL.set_ylabel('continuum')

    s = sigspec(fl, iv, nsm)
    axR.plot(W, s, lw=0.6, color='0.2')
    axR.axhline(0, color='0.6', lw=.6)
    for y0 in (3, -3):
        axR.axhline(y0, color='C0', lw=.7, ls=':')
    m = np.nanmax(np.abs(s[(W > 3700) & (W < hi_x)]))
    axR.set_ylim(-min(m * 1.15, 30), min(m * 1.15, 30))
    axR.set_title(f'significance, filter matched at {nsm} px '
                  f'({nsm*0.8:.0f} A)   dotted = +-3 sigma', fontsize=8.5,
                  loc='left')
    axR.set_ylabel('sigma')

    for ax in (axL, axR):
        for (nm, l0), lo_ in zip(lines, lam):
            ax.axvline(lo_, color='C3', lw=.9, alpha=.7)
            ax.annotate(nm, (lo_, 1.0), xycoords=('data', 'axes fraction'),
                        ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=7, color='C3')
        ax.set_xlim(3600, hi_x)
for ax in axes[-1]:
    ax.set_xlabel('observed wavelength (A)')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Result: 16/16 types correct. Redshift by eye landed inside tol=0.003 for the stars, the quasars and the ELG (0.811 read against 0.81287).

Two of these four are worth dwelling on.

Panel 2 is a targeting error caught by looking. DESI_TARGET says QSO. The spectrum shows the Balmer series in absorption at rest — Hδ, Hγ, Hβ, Hα all where an unshifted star puts them — and the catalogue redshift is −0.0002. It is an A-type star. This is not a catalogue defect: quasar targeting is a point-source colour cut, and blue stars occupy the same colour box.

Row 4 is a failure of my rendering, not of the data. I declined it in round 1 because a single linear panel scaled to the noise cannot show a 4000 Å break or a percent-deep absorption line. In the left column the break is plain, and Ca II H+K sit in the 4320/4360 dip. How you look is part of the measurement.

The two columns are not decoration. The first version of this figure drew all four as raw flux with the lines marked, which shows the quasar and the ELG honestly and merely asserts the star and the galaxy — their evidence is invisible at a scale set by the noise. The right column also uses a filter width matched to each object (61 px for broad quasar lines, 31 for a star's pressure-broadened Balmer, 9 for nebular emission); getting that width wrong is the single mistake behind three separate bugs in this project, section 21.

Which panel carries the evidence depends on the object, and that is the point. Rows 2, 3 and 4 are settled by the right column — Hδ/Hγ/Hβ at −4.5, −4.5 and −3.5σ for the star, [O II] at 25σ and [O III] at 28σ for the ELG, Ca II H+K at −3.5σ for the galaxy. Row 1 is settled by the left column: its significance panel swings hard because a 301 px continuum cannot follow the Lyman-α forest, so everything blueward of Lyα becomes residual. That is an artefact of continuum subtraction on a broad-line object, not weak evidence — the quasar's four lines are the strongest features anywhere in this figure.

19. Where the eye stops — and why it is not a matter of effort¶

The blind test failed on passive galaxies. That is not carelessness. Measured at the catalogue redshift — the best possible case, since the answer is handed over — this is the peak matched-filter significance of each individual feature:

class Ca II K Ca II H G band Mg b Na D [O II] Hα [O III]
LRG 2.7 / 40% 2.9 / 47% 2.0 / 20% 2.1 / 28% 3.9 / 67% 2.2 / 32% 3.7 / 55% 1.7 / 19%
BGS 1.9 / 17% 2.4 / 32% 1.7 / 14% 2.0 / 24% 2.7 / 45% 3.2 / 54% 15.7 / 79% 2.2 / 33%
ELG 1.3 / 1% 1.5 / 5% 1.4 / 2% 1.3 / 1% 1.6 / 0% 11.2 / 82% 6.7 / 64% 9.1 / 78%

(median |σ| / fraction above 3σ, p060; p100 and p020 agree to a few percent — these are properties of the object, and the SNR levels are observation depth.)

An LRG's strongest single feature is Na D at 3.9σ, yet LRG redshifts are measured at 98.5%. A passive galaxy's redshift is not located in any visible feature; it exists only in the coherent sum of hundreds of weak ones.

Drawn in units of σ, so the noise floor is flat and every feature is on the same scale:

In [18]:
NSM = 9
def sigspec(fl, iv):
    good = iv > 0
    num = uniform_filter1d(np.where(good, fl * iv, 0.), 151)
    den = uniform_filter1d(np.where(good, iv, 0.), 151)
    cont = np.where(den > 0, num / np.maximum(den, 1e-30), 0.)
    res = np.where(good, fl - cont, 0.)
    a = uniform_filter1d(res * np.where(good, iv, 0.), NSM) * NSM
    b = np.sqrt(np.maximum(uniform_filter1d(np.where(good, iv, 0.), NSM) * NSM, 1e-30))
    return a / b

SHOW = [('p060', 7854, 'LRG, z=0.56199', [('CaK', 3933.7), ('CaH', 3968.5),
                                          ('Mgb', 5175.), ('NaD', 5895.6)]),
        ('p060', 7951, 'ELG, z=0.81287', [('[OII]', 3728.5), ('[OIII]', 5008.2)])]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(13, 6))
for ax, (lv, row, lab, lines) in zip(axes, SHOW):
    fl, iv = getspec(lv, row)
    s = sigspec(fl, iv)
    zc = np.load(f'{BASE}/blind_{lv}.npz', allow_pickle=True)['zA'][row]
    ax.plot(W, s, lw=0.6, color='0.2')
    for lvl, st in ((3, ':'), (-3, ':')):
        ax.axhline(lvl, color='C0', lw=.8, ls=st)
    ax.axhline(0, color='C3', lw=.6)
    for nm, lam in lines:
        ax.axvline(lam * (1 + zc), color='C3', lw=.9, alpha=.7)
        ax.annotate(nm, (lam * (1 + zc), 1.0), xycoords=('data', 'axes fraction'),
                    ha='center', va='bottom', fontsize=7, color='C3')
    ax.set_ylim(-13, 13); ax.set_xlim(3600, 9000)
    ax.set_ylabel('significance (sigma)')
    ax.set_title(f'{lab}   (dotted lines at +-3 sigma)', fontsize=9, loc='left')
axes[-1].set_xlabel('observed wavelength (A)')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

The ELG's [O II] and [O III] stand far outside the ±3σ band. The LRG's marked features are inside the noise — every one of them. Its redshift is nonetheless recovered, by the template fit, from the sum.

This is the mechanism behind the previously measured 4.8-point loss of image-first routing to formula-first (section 13). It was an information limit all along, not a modelling failure.

Exactly where the redshift is, per pixel¶

The argument above is indirect — it shows the features are weak, not where the redshift comes from. The direct statement is Fisher information. A pixel constrains the redshift in proportion to

I(lambda)  =  ivar(lambda) * ( d model / d z )^2

A bright pixel whose model does not move when z moves carries no redshift information at all. So "where is the redshift" has an exact per-pixel answer, and the cumulative curve says how much of the spectrum is needed to pin it down. Red shading below is that information; the right-hand panel is its running total.

In [19]:
import engine as E, templates as T
WOBS = np.exp(E.LNOBS)
S2 = T.stage2_models(); NAMES = [m.name for m in S2]
NPOLY = 8
POLY = np.vstack([np.polynomial.legendre.legval(np.linspace(-1, 1, E.ND),
                                                [0]*i + [1]) for i in range(NPOLY)])

def _design(m, z):
    lam = E.LNOBS - np.log(1 + z)
    A = np.empty((E.ND, m.K + NPOLY))
    for a in range(m.K):
        A[:, a] = np.interp(lam, E.LNREST, m.B[a], left=0., right=0.)
    A[:, m.K:] = POLY.T
    cov = np.interp(lam, E.LNREST, m.cov.astype(float), left=0., right=0.) > .5
    return A, cov

def zinfo(fl, iv, z, mi):
    # per-pixel Fisher information for redshift, amplitudes held fixed
    fh, w = E.prepare(fl, iv, [0.0])
    y = fh[0.0]; s = np.median(np.abs(y)) + 1e-9
    y = y / s; w = w * s * s; sw = np.sqrt(w)
    m = S2[mi]
    A, cov = _design(m, z)
    Aw = A * (sw * cov)[:, None]
    c, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(Aw, y * sw * cov, rcond=1e-8)
    dz = 3e-4 * (1 + z)
    dmdz = (_design(m, z + dz)[0] @ c - _design(m, z - dz)[0] @ c) / (2 * dz)
    return y, A @ c, w * dmdz**2 * cov, cov

SHOW = [('p060', 7951, 'ELG   z = 0.813'), ('p060', 7854, 'LRG   z = 0.562'),
        ('p100', 2096, 'QSO   z = 3.105'), ('p060', 2438, 'STAR  z = 0.000')]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 2, figsize=(15, 12),
                         gridspec_kw={'width_ratios': [2.1, 1]})
for (lv, row, lab), (axA, axB) in zip(SHOW, axes):
    d = np.load(f'{BASE}/blind_{lv}.npz', allow_pickle=True)
    z = float(d['z'][row])
    fl, iv = getspec(lv, row)
    fam = ['STAR', 'BGS', 'LRG', 'ELG', 'QSO'][int(np.argmax(d['bd'][row]))]
    mi = next((i for i, n in enumerate(NAMES) if n.rstrip('a') == fam), 0)
    y, mp, I, cov = zinfo(fl, iv, z, mi)
    frac = np.cumsum(I) / max(I.sum(), 1e-30)
    axA.plot(WOBS, y, lw=.5, color='0.65', label='data')
    axA.plot(WOBS, np.where(cov, mp, np.nan), lw=.9, color='C0', label='model')
    ax2 = axA.twinx()
    Ip = uniform_filter1d(I, 5)
    ax2.fill_between(WOBS, 0, Ip / max(Ip.max(), 1e-30), color='C3', alpha=.45, lw=0)
    ax2.set_ylim(0, 1.05); ax2.set_yticks([])
    lo, hi = np.percentile(y, [1, 99.5]); pad = .35 * (hi - lo)
    axA.set_ylim(lo - pad, hi + pad); axA.set_xlim(3600, 9800)
    axA.set_title(lab + '    red = redshift information per pixel',
                  fontsize=9, loc='left')
    axA.legend(fontsize=7, loc='upper right')
    cum = np.cumsum(np.sort(I)[::-1]) / max(I.sum(), 1e-30)
    n50 = int(np.searchsorted(cum, .5)) + 1; n90 = int(np.searchsorted(cum, .9)) + 1
    axB.plot(WOBS, 100 * frac, lw=1.4, color='C3')
    axB.axhline(50, color='0.7', lw=.7, ls=':')
    axB.set_xlim(3600, 9800); axB.set_ylim(0, 100)
    axB.set_ylabel('% of redshift information')
    axB.set_title('half of it lives in %d pixels (%.2f%%);\n90%% in %d (%.1f%%)'
                  % (n50, 100*n50/E.ND, n90, 100*n90/E.ND),
                  fontsize=8.5, loc='left')
    print('%-18s model=%-6s  half in %5d px   90%% in %5d px'
          % (lab, NAMES[mi], n50, n90))
for ax in axes[-1]:
    ax.set_xlabel('observed wavelength (A)')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

ELG   z = 0.813    model=ELG     half in     7 px   90% in    26 px
LRG   z = 0.562    model=LRG     half in   175 px   90% in  1425 px
QSO   z = 3.105    model=QSO     half in   356 px   90% in  2226 px

object half the redshift information lives in 90% in
ELG z=0.813 7 pixels (0.10%) 26 (0.4%)
LRG z=0.562 175 (2.61%) 1425 (21.3%)
STAR z=0.000 190 (2.84%) 1567 (23.4%)
QSO z=3.105 356 (5.32%) 2226 (33.3%)

An ELG's redshift is written in 7 of 7781 pixels. The information spikes sit on [O II] at 6760, Hβ at 8800 and [O III] at 9070 and nowhere else — the cumulative curve is a three-step staircase. Mask those three places and the redshift is gone entirely.

A passive galaxy is the opposite. The LRG's information is spread over dozens of weak features between 5800 and 9500, its curve climbs smoothly, and it takes 1425 pixels to reach 90% — 25 times more of the spectrum than the ELG needs. There is nowhere you can point and say the redshift is here.

This is the quantitative form of the claim above, and it settles why the eye succeeds on one and fails on the other. It is not a matter of effort, and not of rendering: for a passive galaxy there is no single place where the redshift is written. It is also why a matched filter beats a picture here, and why image-first routing loses 4.8 points (section 13) — the filter can sum 1425 pixels coherently and the eye cannot.

20. The imaging label is not the truth — and neither am I¶

val_80k carries SPECTYPE, an actual spectroscopic classification, so for once the disagreements can be adjudicated rather than merely counted. (SPECTYPE is Redrock-derived and is used here only for scoring, exactly as the catalogue redshift is — nothing in the pipeline reads it.)

Whole sample, n=20,000: my class from the spectrum 95.61%, DESI_TARGET 96.34%. Imaging wins — but only because of the objects where the spectrum says nothing.

The strongest case for reading the spectrum is quasars: imaging is right only 73.7% of the time.

And my own mirror-image weakness, stated plainly: I call 659 galaxies (5.0%) quasars — 540 of them ELG targets, concentrated at z>1 (16.0% of galaxies at z=1.3–1.7), where [O II] has moved into the bright sky and Hβ/[O III] have left the range, leaving a blue continuum that a power law fits happily. Their median significance is 0.94 against 8.33. The redshift is still right 86.5% of the time at the same precision (median |Δz|/(1+z) 0.00004 vs 0.00003) — the class error barely touches the deliverable.

21. The blind spot this exposed: my confidence measure could not see stars¶

Chasing why ~4% of quasar targets are stars led to a defect in the confidence measure itself. best_feature_sig asked STAR for Ca II H and K only.

A hot star has no Ca II H and K. Its evidence is the Balmer series in absorption — and hot blue stars are exactly what contaminates the quasar colour box. The measure was blind to the population the decline rules mishandle.

Two gaps, both already half-built in the codebase:

  • G_BALM_ABS and G_CAT were defined in classform.py and never used
  • Hδ/Hγ/Hβ/Hα existed only at 90 km/s — the nebular width. Stellar Balmer lines are pressure-broadened, and the analytic star template already used 900 km/s. Measuring a 900 km/s line with a 90 km/s filter is the same error as a high-pass narrower than its feature (section 6).

Worse: I had previously "fixed" the symptom by dropping T3['STAR'] to 0.5 — compensating for a broken measurement instead of repairing it.

The picture makes it obvious:

What it was worth¶

Both adopted changes are strictly dominant: zero losses at every level.

dataset before after tier-1 paired
p100 93.6% @ 97.36% 93.7% @ 97.37% 74.2% → 74.4% +2 −0
p080 86.2% @ 97.53% 87.7% @ 97.55% 53.9% → 60.6% +132 −0
p060 86.0% @ 97.69% 87.5% @ 97.71% 52.1% → 58.1% +129 −0
p040 86.0% @ 97.61% 87.6% @ 97.64% 51.4% → 57.5% +143 −0
p020 85.0% @ 97.15% 86.5% @ 97.20% 52.6% → 57.4% +139 −0
val_80k (sv3) 91.6% @ 99.24% 94.8% @ 99.26% 60.7% → 72.0% @ 99.70% +642 −0 (+25.3σ)

val_80k is a different survey with no threshold tuned on it, so it is the real test — and there the whole gain is stars: STAR answered 88.4% → 99.2% at an unchanged 99.84% accuracy. 11.6% of stars had been declined despite being measured perfectly.

Decline rule B was fixed by exemption, not by rewrite. Rule B ("a non-STAR target that returns z≈0 must be wrong") fires 2715 times over six levels and discards a correct answer 728 times — more good than bad at every level except p000. But replacing it wholesale does not pay: any rule of the form "z≈0 and weak evidence → decline" also starts declining genuine stellar targets the old rule never touched, and the two cancel (+19 −14, +12 −23, +18 −18). What works is the minimal change — keep the rule, exempt objects that plainly show a star at 4σ. It can only un-decline, so it cannot lose, and it gains +12 to +17 per level with zero losses.

22. The z = 1.45–1.70 degeneracy, identified¶

Section 17 found that p000 puts 52% of stellar targets at large redshift, 65.8% of them piled into z=1.65–1.70. That was treated as a p000 pathology. It is not. The same failure exists at every depth — 2 cases at p100, 3 at p080, 3 at p060, 2 at p040, 14 at p020 — and every one of them lands in z = 1.45–1.70.

Rendering them settles what they are, and the overlay shows the mechanism:

The Balmer ladder is at rest — this is an A-type star. At z≈1.55 a rest-UV template puts C IV 1549 at 3951 and C III] 1909 at 4868, landing on Hε/Hδ and Hβ.

The first version of this section stopped there and declared that the fit matches the Balmer confluence to the UV emission complex. That was a coincidence of position presented as a mechanism. Two lines being in the same place does not show that a fitter chooses z≈1.55 because of it.

Testing it properly, after two designs that could not¶

The obvious test — mask the Balmer lines, refit, see if the solution moves — failed twice, and how it failed is the useful part.

Attempt 1 selected objects by where the fit lands. Across all six levels only 13 of 12,000 stellar targets send my fit to z = 1.35–1.85. A test on 13 objects returned +1.4σ and could never have resolved anything.

Attempt 2 lacked a control. "Remove the cause and the answer moves" is not evidence: removing any information moves a fit. The control has to remove the same number of pixels somewhere else.

The redesign asks about the χ² surface, not the outcome. The claim is not about where the fit lands — it is that a quasar template develops a spurious peak near z≈1.55 on a stellar spectrum, built out of the Balmer lines. Asked that way every star yields a measurement, and n goes from 13 to 400.

The trap is real and it is enormous. Masking the Balmer lines leaves 17.4% of the spurious peak; masking the same 761 pixels elsewhere leaves 99.7%. Paired, that is +82σ, and the Balmer mask cut the peak more in 396 of 400 stars. About 83% of a Δχ² ≈ 3400 false solution is built out of hydrogen absorption lines.

And then the correction that actually mattered¶

Proving the trap exists did not prove it explains what I had used it to explain.
MWS targets my pipeline puts in z = 1.35–1.85 0.05–0.15%, flat at every level including p000
MWS targets the catalogue puts above z = 0.01 at p000 52.3%

My pipeline is immune at every depth. Not because the trap is absent — it is right there in the χ² surface, worth 3400 — but because the stellar template wins the comparison (the QSO family wins on only 0.8–3.6% of stellar targets). The defence is the presence of a better-fitting alternative, not the absence of a trap.

So the z = 1.65 pile-up is a property of the catalogue's fit, and I have been explaining another fitter's failure with a mechanism demonstrated in mine. This trap is the natural candidate — it is exactly what a rest-UV template does to an A star — but that is an inference about a system I cannot inspect. It is not shown here, and the earlier draft of this section was wrong to say it was.

I also proposed, and refuted within one command, that "the STAR-versus-QSO margin shrinks with depth, which is why p000 is epidemic": the margin does not fall monotonically, and my landing rate is flat across all six levels.

What this section can claim: the Balmer/UV degeneracy exists, its size is measured, and it is defeated by template competition rather than avoided. What it cannot: why the catalogue falls into something that looks like it.

(Section 17's composition test and the 47.8% ↔ 52.35% agreement in section 21 stand on their own — they show the reference is untrustworthy for those objects without needing any mechanism at all.)

A closing confirmation, from an unrelated instrument¶

With the stellar evidence added, the pipeline now answers 99.2% of p000 stellar targets, at a measured accuracy of 47.8%.

Section 17 established, by a completely independent composition test, that 52.35% of p000 MWS targets are placed by the catalogue outside the stellar range. 100 − 52.35 = 47.65.

Two unrelated measurements agreeing to one decimal place. The pipeline now answers essentially every star and is scored wrong by exactly the fraction the catalogue has corrupted.

23. What Part II changed, and what it did not¶

The redshift never used the imaging label. Running the whole pipeline with DESI_TARGET removed gives redshifts that are bit for bit identical — 93.23 / 90.54 / 90.82 / 90.51 / 89.59 / 48.83 across the six levels, matching production exactly. The label only ever entered the confidence stage.

Kept — two changes, both zero-loss at every level:

  1. stellar Balmer absorption at 900 km/s and the Ca II triplet added to STAR's evidence set
  2. decline rule B given a 4σ stellar exemption

Rejected — five, each tested and measured:

change result
rewrite rule B entirely +19 −14, +12 −23, +18 −18 — cancels out
choose line groups by spectral class instead of target class ±0 at every level
use the spectral class as an unconditional prior loses to imaging on sv3
template winning margin as a confidence signal 96.00% even at 60% coverage
class disagreement as a decline criterion helps at p100, hurts mid-levels

Three corrections to claims made during this work:

  • "sig2 ranks no better than sig" — true at p100, and wrong everywhere else: it is worth a consistent +1.5 points at p080–p020. I had tested only the one level where it does not matter.
  • the "variant A" baseline in the first comparison was not production — its significance was already computed under the spectral class.
  • the headline table in Part I quotes p080 at 82.9% answered. That figure predates the BGS/STAR threshold loosening in decide.py; recomputed with the current code the correct baseline is 86.2%.

The lesson that repeats. Three of this project's findings are now the same error in different clothes: a high-pass narrower than its feature, a y-scale set by the noise instead of the signal, and a 90 km/s filter on a 900 km/s line. Each time the information was present and the instrument could not see it. Failing to measure something is not evidence that it is absent — and the way to catch it has been the same every time: render the spectrum and look.

24. What kind of error is left¶

The pipeline is at 97.4-97.7% on what it answers. The useful question is not how to push that number but what kind of thing the remaining errors are — because precision failures, selection failures and missing candidates need completely different work.

Every remaining error is a selection failure. None are precision failures.¶

Fisher information gives the Cramér-Rao bound on the redshift, σ_z = 1/√(ΣI), which is the best precision any unbiased estimator could reach on that spectrum. Measured at my own answer, the median σ_z is 4.6-6.8 × 10⁻⁵, i.e. 14-20 km/s — about 50 times tighter than the 900 km/s pass mark.

Expressing every error in those units:

level wrong median |Δz|/σ_z within 5σ_z beyond 100σ_z
p100 677 3470 0.0% 94.5%
p080 946 4434 0.0% 94.9%
p060 918 4723 0.0% 94.3%
p040 949 4548 0.0% 95.3%
p020 1041 4781 0.0% 95.1%
p000 5117 13362 0.0% 98.7%

Correct answers sit at 1.9-2.9 σ_z, as theory says they should. Wrong answers are three to thirteen thousand σ_z away, and not one error in 12,000 is within 5σ_z of the truth. The two populations do not overlap at all.

So no local uncertainty can ever flag these, because at the wrong peak the fit is exactly as well determined as at the right one. Tested directly — the Cramér-Rao bound is a worse confidence signal than feature significance at every level and every coverage:

In [25]:
def acc_at(score, ok, frac):
    n = int(round(frac * len(ok)))
    return 100 * ok[np.argsort(-score)[:n]].mean()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4))
fr = [.95, .90, .85, .75, .60]
for lv, style in (('p100', '-'), ('p060', '--')):
    b = np.load(f'{BASE}/blind_{lv}.npz', allow_pickle=True)
    c = np.load(f'{BASE}/crb_{lv}.npz')
    z, zA, sig2, sigz = b['z'], b['zA'], b['sig2'], c['sigz']
    ok = np.abs((z - zA) / (1 + zA)) < 0.003
    g = np.isfinite(sigz) & (sigz > 0)
    z, zA, sig2, sigz, ok = z[g], zA[g], sig2[g], sigz[g], ok[g]
    ax[0].plot(fr, [acc_at(sig2, ok, f) for f in fr], 'o' + style, color='C0',
               label=f'{lv} feature significance')
    ax[0].plot(fr, [acc_at(1 / sigz, ok, f) for f in fr], 's' + style,
               color='C3', label=f'{lv} 1/sigma_z (Cramer-Rao)')
    if lv == 'p060':
        pull = np.abs(z - zA) / np.maximum(sigz, 1e-12)
        ax[1].hist(np.log10(np.clip(pull[ok], 1e-2, 1e7)), bins=60,
                   color='C0', alpha=.7, label='correct answers')
        ax[1].hist(np.log10(np.clip(pull[~ok], 1e-2, 1e7)), bins=60,
                   color='C3', alpha=.7, label='wrong answers')
ax[0].set_xlabel('fraction answered'); ax[0].set_ylabel('accuracy (%)')
ax[0].legend(fontsize=7); ax[0].grid(alpha=.3); ax[0].invert_xaxis()
ax[0].set_title('theoretical precision is the WORSE confidence signal',
                fontsize=9, loc='left')
ax[1].axvline(np.log10(5), color='0.3', ls=':')
ax[1].set_xlabel('log10 ( |dz| / sigma_z )'); ax[1].set_ylabel('objects')
ax[1].legend(fontsize=8)
ax[1].set_title('p060: the two populations do not overlap\n'
                '(dotted line = 5 sigma_z)', fontsize=9, loc='left')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Where the wrong peaks come from¶

If the error is selection, there are only three places it can arise: the true redshift was never generated as a candidate, it was generated and ranked below another, or the scoring function genuinely prefers the wrong answer. Measured by forcing the true redshift into the scorer:

level wrong true z on the shortlist true z wins when forced in
p100 677 52.6% 11.7%
p080 946 39.9% 11.4%
p060 918 42.0% 11.9%
p040 949 40.4% 13.2%
p020 1041 41.4% 15.1%

Only 11-15% of errors are candidate-generation failures. For the other 85-89% the truth is offered to the scorer and still loses — so no improvement to stage 1 or to ranking can touch them. On those objects the best fit is worth only Δχ² ≈ 43-79 (these are information-starved spectra), and the wrong answer beats the truth by 35-53% of that, which is 2.7-4.4 × √χ² — a real margin, not a coin flip. The templates genuinely prefer the wrong redshift.

Most of that never reaches the user¶

level wrong caught by the decline rule leaked (wrong and answered)
p100 677 63.5% 247 per 10,000
p080 946 77.3% 215
p060 918 78.2% 200
p040 949 78.2% 207
p020 1041 76.8% 242

The decline rule removes about three quarters of all errors. What leaks is 2.0-2.5% of the sample, and it has a completely different character from what is caught:

leaked caught
median feature significance 3.5-5.0 0.7
share that is tier 1 (confident) 19-36% 0%
catastrophic (>0.02) 71-75% 96%

The errors that survive are confident ones. They carry 3.5-5σ of genuine feature significance and a fifth of them are tier 1. That is not an information-starved spectrum — a real line is being detected and assigned to the wrong transition.

In [26]:
LINES = {'Lya': 1215.67, 'CIV': 1549.48, 'CIII]': 1908.73, 'MgII': 2799.12,
         '[OII]': 3728.48, '[NeIII]': 3869.86, 'CaK': 3934.78, 'Hd': 4102.89,
         'Hg': 4341.68, 'Hb': 4862.68, '[OIII]4959': 4960.30,
         '[OIII]5007': 5008.24, 'Ha': 6564.61, '[SII]': 6725.48,
         'break4000': 4000.0}
NM = list(LINES)
pr = sorted((LINES[a] / LINES[b], f'{a} read as {b}')
            for a in NM for b in NM if a != b)
Rr = np.array([p[0] for p in pr]); LB = [p[1] for p in pr]

zm, zt = [], []
for lv in LEVELS[:5]:
    d = np.load(f'{BASE}/prod2_{lv}.npz', allow_pickle=True)
    z, zA, tier = d['z'], d['zA'], d['tier']
    ok = np.abs((z - zA) / (1 + zA)) < 0.003
    k = (~ok) & (tier < 3) & (np.abs(z - zA) / (1 + zA) > 0.02)
    zm.append(z[k]); zt.append(zA[k])
zm = np.concatenate(zm); zt = np.concatenate(zt)
r = (1 + zm) / (1 + zt)

def expl(v, tol):
    j = np.argmin(np.abs(Rr[None, :] - v[:, None]), axis=1)
    return np.abs(Rr[j] - v) / v < tol, j

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
tols = [0.01, 0.005, 0.002, 0.001, 0.0005]
obs, nul = [], []
for t in tols:
    obs.append(100 * expl(r, t)[0].mean())
    nn = []
    for _ in range(200):
        rn = (1 + zm) / (1 + zt[rng.permutation(len(zt))])
        m = (rn > r.min()) & (rn < r.max())
        if m.sum():
            nn.append(100 * expl(rn[m], t)[0].mean())
    nul.append(np.mean(nn))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4))
x = 100 * np.array(tols)
ax[0].plot(x, obs, 'o-', color='C0', label='observed')
ax[0].plot(x, nul, 's--', color='0.5', label='permutation null')
ax[0].fill_between(x, nul, obs, color='C3', alpha=.25, label='excess')
ax[0].set_xscale('log'); ax[0].set_xlabel('match tolerance (%)')
ax[0].set_ylabel('% "explained" by one line swap')
ax[0].legend(fontsize=8); ax[0].grid(alpha=.3)
ax[0].set_title('the null must be able to fail:\nat 1% tolerance chance alone '
                'scores 87.5%', fontsize=9, loc='left')

good, j = expl(r, 0.001)
from collections import Counter
cnt = Counter(LB[jj] for jj, g in zip(j, good) if g)
top = cnt.most_common(8)[::-1]
ax[1].barh([t[0] for t in top], [t[1] for t in top], color='C0')
ax[1].set_xlabel(f'objects (of {len(r)} leaked catastrophic errors)')
ax[1].set_title('which lines get confused, at 0.1% tolerance',
                fontsize=9, loc='left')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f'n = {len(r)};  excess over the permutation null at 0.05% tolerance: '
      f'{obs[-1]-nul[-1]:.1f} points')

n = 732;  excess over the permutation null at 0.05% tolerance: 20.2 points

About 20% of the leaked catastrophic errors are single-line misidentifications — the excess over the permutation null settles at 18-20 points as the tolerance tightens, reaching +19.6σ at 0.05%. The confusions are all among the strong emission lines: [O III] 5007 read as [O II], [O II] read as Hα, [O III] read as [S II] or Hα.

The first version of this test claimed 93.7%. It matched against every ratio of 15 line wavelengths — 210 values densely covering the range — within 1%, where chance alone scores 87.5%. That is the third time in this report a test was built whose null hypothesis also passes (see section 22). The fix is always the same: tighten until chance agreement is small, and use a null that preserves the marginals and destroys only the thing under test.

What this says about where to work¶

finding consequence
no error is a precision failure better noise models, weighting, LSF work: nothing to gain
only 11-15% are missing candidates improving stage-1 recall: caps at ~1.5 points
85-89% the scorer prefers the wrong z the templates themselves are the limit
the decline rule catches 3/4 of errors refusal remains the best tool, as in section 14
~20% of leaks are line confusion line ratios and the absence of companion lines — not stronger single-line detection

The remaining error is a discrete problem — which peak, not how precisely. That is worth stating because most of the tempting work (finer sampling, better noise treatment, sharper filters) addresses the continuous problem, which is already 50 times better than it needs to be.

Part III — From the survey files, and what "SNR" means¶

Parts I and II worked from pre-made HDF5 extracts. This part goes to DR1 itself: the 28.4-million-row catalogue and the per-healpix coadd files, with the three camera arms still separate.

25. Combining the arms, the official way¶

DESI delivers B, R and Z separately. They sit on a common 0.8 Å grid — B 3600–5800 (2751 px), R 5760–7620 (2326), Z 7520–9824 (2881) — so their wavelength values coincide exactly in the two overlap regions, and the merged grid is simply their union: 7781 points, which is the grid the earlier HDF5 files were already on.

Following desispec.coaddition.coadd_cameras, non-overlapping pixels are taken directly and overlapping ones are accumulated inverse-variance weighted. For a pixel covered by one arm the second reduces to the first, so a single expression covers the whole spectrum:

$$f(\lambda)=\frac{\sum_i \mathrm{iv}_i(\lambda)\,f_i(\lambda)}{\sum_i \mathrm{iv}_i(\lambda)},\qquad \mathrm{iv}(\lambda)=\sum_i \mathrm{iv}_i(\lambda),\qquad \mathrm{mask}=\bigvee_i \mathrm{mask}_i$$

with masked pixels carrying zero weight, which is what makes the sum safe to write unconditionally. This lives in speclib.py together with the two views that were established to work — an inverse-variance weighted continuum, and a significance spectrum whose filter width is matched to the feature — so it does not have to be rewritten each session.

26. Three different things are called SNR¶

A batch of 100 targets (20 per class, drawn across the depth range) makes the distinction unavoidable. Median TSNR2_BGS was 1742 and median TSNR2_QSO 7.6, a factor 229 — while the per-pixel SNR went the other way, 2.97 against 10.54. The columns are each normalised to their own tracer template and are not comparable between tracers.

quantity property of
TSNR2_X the observation — exposure, conditions, fibre — weighted for tracer X
SNR per pixel how bright the object is
feature significance whether the redshift can actually be measured

STAR   TSNR2-SNR/px -0.002   TSNR2-sig +0.258   SNR/px-sig +0.706
BGS    TSNR2-SNR/px +0.357   TSNR2-sig +0.247   SNR/px-sig +0.214
LRG    TSNR2-SNR/px +0.207   TSNR2-sig +0.334   SNR/px-sig +0.518
ELG    TSNR2-SNR/px +0.530   TSNR2-sig +0.400   SNR/px-sig +0.498
QSO    TSNR2-SNR/px +0.261   TSNR2-sig +0.294   SNR/px-sig +0.332

The STAR row is the clean decomposition. TSNR2 is exactly uncorrelated with how bright a star is (−0.002) — a longer exposure cannot change that — but is correlated with how well its features are measured (+0.26). An observational quantity can only explain the observational part of the variance.

Which SNR predicts readability depends on the class: STAR 0.71, LRG 0.52, ELG 0.50, QSO 0.33, and BGS 0.21. BGS is a mixture — passive galaxies whose evidence is the 4000 Å break and star-forming ones whose evidence is Hα — and averaging two mechanisms washes the relation out.

Two claims of mine that this refuted¶

"An ELG's line detectability is anti-correlated with its brightness." Measured on the 20-object batch: r = −0.43, with a tidy equivalent-width story ready to explain it. At n = 2000 per level it is +0.34 to +0.38 at all five levels, and the brightness quintiles rise monotonically (right panel above). At n = 20, |r| > 0.44 is needed for p < 0.05; the anti-correlation was a fluctuation.

"TSNR2 predicts nothing." Also from n = 20 — and wrong a second way. Measured within one SNR level the correlation really is ~0 (+0.081, −0.031, −0.005, −0.012), but those levels are TSNR2 percentile bands, so TSNR2 has almost no range left inside one. The correlation vanishes by construction, not by physics. Across its full range it is +0.25 to +0.40.

27. The 4000 Å break is a shape, not a feature¶

Ten bright-programme LRG targets, rendered and read by eye. The line filter (70 km/s) showed nothing above 3σ on any of them, while the break was plainly visible in the continuum panel — which looks exactly like a filter-width bug, a 3-pixel filter on a ~500-pixel feature. So a break filter was built.

It failed twice.

  • A first difference — mean flux red of λ minus mean flux blue of λ — fires everywhere on a continuum that rises to the red, which all of these have. It returned >5σ for 100% of stars and quasars. It was measuring slope.
  • A second difference, which cancels any linear trend exactly, then fires on every genuinely localised feature instead: Balmer absorption in a star, broad lines in a quasar.

Both were caught by running them on the other classes as a control. Neither would ever have exposed itself.

Adjudicating against the catalogue settled who was right:

A 77.0% match rate against a 25.6 ± 4.7% uniform null is +10.9σ, so the filter genuinely finds real spectral features. It just almost never finds the break. Per class the median rest wavelength it locks onto is BGS 6534 (Hα), ELG 5033 ([O III]/Hβ), LRG 5867 (the Mg b – Na D metal complex).

(Six of the ten LRG failures shared one factor, (1+z_f)/(1+z_true) = 1.302–1.316, and I first read that as Mg b — 4000 × 1.31 = 5240 against Mg b 5177, consistent at 1.2%. But the population median for LRG is Na D. Six objects cannot name a single line.)

So the 4000 Å break is not a feature that can be pointed at — it is a shape. Any statistic looking for localised structure at the 100–350 Å scale will find the genuinely localised things and step straight over a several-hundred-ångström change in continuum level.

Why the eye won 8:1: it was not measuring an edge. It was matching the whole continuum shape — blue depression, rise, red plateau — which is a multi-scale judgement, i.e. a template match by another name. That is the same conclusion section 24 reached from the opposite direction: an LRG's redshift is spread over ~1425 pixels, so no local statistic can carry it.

And the part the eye cannot do¶

The same batch shows the reverse just as sharply. Of 20 ELG targets, four were solved instantly and unambiguously from a single number — the fixed wavelength ratio [O III] 5007 / [O II] 3728 = 1.343. Two lines at that spacing fix the redshift with no template at all.

Three others carried exactly one line, and one line is irreducibly ambiguous: the same observed wavelength gives z = 1.227 as [O II], 0.658 as [O III], or 0.264 as Hα. That is the misidentification failure of section 24, met in the wild rather than in a statistic.

The two classes fail in opposite directions. An ELG's redshift is in a few pixels and is either present or absent. A passive galaxy's is in the whole continuum and is never in any one place. A single instrument cannot serve both, which is the entire argument for the two-stage architecture of section 4.

28. The survey equalises evidence, not photons¶

Section 26 left a puzzle. TSNR2 correlates with feature significance (0.25–0.40) but is exactly uncorrelated with how bright a star is (−0.002), and the per-pixel SNR of a batch bore no relation to its TSNR2. A second batch of 100 targets — drawn to span the dark and bright programmes rather than one of them by accident — resolves it.

Dark time is not spent measuring the same objects better. Comparing the same target class across the two programmes:

class ΔTSNR2 ΔSNR/px Δline σ Δmedian z
STAR +5798 +15.5 +1.8 0.000
LRG +66.5 −1.35 −0.8 +0.407
ELG +95.9 −2.11 +2.4 +0.755
QSO +25.7 −6.59 −17.5 −0.183

Stars behave the way intuition expects — same objects, more photons, SNR per pixel doubles from 16.9 to 32.4, redshift unchanged at zero. Every extragalactic tracer does the opposite. Median redshift moves 0.405 → 0.811 for LRG and 0.450 → 1.204 for ELG, and the per-pixel SNR falls. The extra photons go into reaching further, not into measuring better.

And what stays constant is the evidence:

In [29]:

                   c=b2['zcat'][k], cmap='viridis', s=55,
                   edgecolor='k', linewidth=.4)
ax[1].scatter(b2['median_snr'][k], b2['line_sig'][k], marker='x',
              color='C3', s=40, label='best line sigma')
plt.colorbar(sc, ax=ax[1], label='catalogue z')
ax[1].axhline(3, color='0.4', ls=':', lw=.9)
ax[1].set_xlabel('SNR per pixel'); ax[1].set_ylabel('significance')
ax[1].legend(fontsize=8, loc='upper left'); ax[1].grid(alpha=.3)
ax[1].set_title('LRG targets: circles = break, crosses = line',
                fontsize=9, loc='left')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

for nm, s, l, br in rows:
    print(f'{nm.replace(chr(10), " "):14s} SNR/px {s:5.2f}   line {l:5.1f}   '
          f'break {br:5.1f}')

LRG bright     SNR/px  2.43   line   4.7   break   8.3
LRG dark       SNR/px  1.08   line   3.9   break   8.8
ELG bright     SNR/px  2.48   line  11.6   break   1.4
ELG dark       SNR/px  0.46   line  13.4   break   1.4

LRG break significance is 8.3σ in bright and 8.8σ in dark, while the per-pixel SNR halves. ELG line significance is 11.6σ and 13.4σ, while the per-pixel SNR drops five-fold, from 2.48 to 0.46. The exposure is longer by exactly enough to integrate away the loss.

So TSNR2_X is not a badly-behaved brightness proxy. It is the template-weighted SNR², the expected significance of tracer X's defining feature — which is why BGS and QSO values differ by a factor 229 and why it predicts feature significance but not brightness. It was never measuring the thing I was comparing it against.

Integration is what makes the faint end work at all. A dark-programme LRG at z = 1.12 has SNR per pixel of 0.62 and no line above 3.8σ, yet its 4000 Å break is detected at 8.4σ — because the break spans ~1054 usable pixels. The naive ceiling would be SNR/px × √N ≈ 32; the realised 8.4 is 27% of that, which is the break's fractional contrast. This is the fact from section 24 — an LRG's redshift is spread over ~1425 pixels — seen from its useful side rather than its costly one.

And the two statistics are cleanly complementary. Over these 40 galaxies:

best line σ break σ
ELG (both programmes) 11.6 – 13.4 1.4
LRG (both programmes) 3.9 – 4.7 8.3 – 8.8

Each class is invisible to the other's instrument. Measuring an ELG with a break statistic returns 1.4σ and measuring an LRG with a line filter returns 3.9σ — and neither number is a statement about the spectrum. It is a statement about the filter, which is the mistake this report has now made in four separate places.

(A useful side effect: an LRG target that is really a star came back at 0.6σ of break while its line statistic said 3.9σ. The right instrument identifies the contaminant; the wrong one reports a plausible-looking number.)

Part IV — A sealed blind test¶

29. Protocol¶

100 fresh spectra from DR1 — the 20 highest-SNR per class, none studied before (the seen list went 300 → 400). The point of this section is that the protocol was tightened until the result could not be flattered.

Selection touched no Redrock product. Only TARGETID, SURVEY, PROGRAM, HEALPIX, COADD_FIBERSTATUS, DESI_TARGET and TSNR2_*. Keep SURVEY=="main", TARGETID>0, COADD_FIBERSTATUS==0; class by DESI_TARGET bits with priority QSO(2) > LRG(0) > ELG(1) > BGS_ANY(60) > MWS_ANY(61)=STAR.

Three details that were wrong in my previous attempt and are fixed here:

  • TARGETID>0 was simply missing before.
  • Dedup by TARGETID, keeping the row with the highest TSNR2_<class> — a target appears on several rows and I had been treating each as a separate object. Explicitly not the *_PRIMARY flags, which rank by ZWARN and would have leaked Redrock into the selection.
  • Two-stage ranking. TSNR2 shortlists 60 per class as a brightness proxy; the final 20 are chosen on measured SNR = median(|flux|·√ivar). TSNR2 is observation depth, not object brightness — section 26.

The renders carry no object information. Only an opaque OBJnnn, in an order shuffled across classes. My previous sheets printed TSNR2 and the programme in every title, both of which leak: programme alone nearly separates BGS/STAR from LRG/ELG/QSO.

The answers were sealed. Z, ZWARN and SPECTYPE for the 100 were written to key_SEALED.json at mode 600 and opened exactly once, by the scoring cell, after all 100 type calls were on disk.

Then, in order: all 100 images were examined; 32 were too faint to call from flux alone and were re-examined through a four-width diagnostic — continuum, blue zoom, 70 km/s and 900/3000 km/s — because a single narrow filter is what hid two stars and a broad-line quasar last time; every type was written down; and only then was the redshift fitted, using only the template family that the visual call selected. No abstention.

30. Every disagreement, with nothing left out¶

The previous version of this section showed four errors and explained them. There were sixteen. Picking the ones I could account for is the selection bias this report keeps warning about, so here is the complete list.

All eleven type disagreements:

id target mine SPECTYPE z Redrock z mine SNR z ok
OBJ007 BGS LRG GALAXY 0.3208 0.3209 4.6 yes
OBJ009 BGS STAR GALAXY 0.1579 −0.0034 4.3 NO
OBJ028 BGS LRG GALAXY 0.2652 0.2652 4.7 yes
OBJ035 BGS LRG GALAXY 0.3200 0.3200 4.9 yes
OBJ037 LRG QSO QSO 0.5258 0.5258 9.7 yes
OBJ046 BGS LRG GALAXY 0.3186 0.3186 5.1 yes
OBJ069 ELG LRG GALAXY 0.4602 0.4603 1.2 yes
OBJ074 BGS LRG GALAXY 0.1323 0.1323 10.4 yes
OBJ078 BGS STAR GALAXY 0.0750 0.0056 6.4 NO
OBJ091 LRG BGS GALAXY 0.3878 0.3880 3.9 yes
OBJ095 LRG BGS GALAXY 0.1225 0.1225 10.6 yes

Nine of the eleven are galaxy-subtype confusions where my redshift is still correct to four decimal places. BGS↔LRG accounts for seven of them — a magnitude cut against a colour cut, which is not a distinction a spectrum carries. Redrock calls all nine simply GALAXY.

OBJ037 is not an error at all. I called QSO on an LRG target and Redrock's SPECTYPE is QSO. The imaging label is the thing that is wrong.

So only two of the hundred are genuine type errors — OBJ009 and OBJ078, both galaxies I read as stars, and both are also redshift failures. Both were cases where the continuum rose and then turned over, and I took the turnover for a stellar continuum rather than a 4000 Å break.

All five redshift failures:

id mine z Redrock z mine ZWARN SNR
OBJ008 LRG 0.9266 0.3298 4 2.7
OBJ009 STAR 0.1579 −0.0034 0 4.3
OBJ016 ELG 0.4793 1.6511 4 1.2
OBJ063 LRG 0.9328 0.3932 646 7.0
OBJ078 STAR 0.0750 0.0056 0 6.4

Three of the five carry ZWARN != 0 — Redrock does not trust its own answer on those three either, so they are disagreements between two uncertain measurements rather than demonstrated failures. Against the 97 rows the reference does vouch for, the redshift is 95/97.

31. The prediction I registered, and why being right proves nothing¶

Before opening the key I wrote down a specific worry: that 18 of my 19 ELG calls came from the group where I could find no usable feature and had fallen back on continuum shape, and that if ELG came out weakest, it would be the same defaulting bias that produced most of my errors in the previous round.

ELG came out as my best class: 19/20 on type, 19/20 on redshift. The flagged group did better than the rest — 18/18 on type, 17/18 on redshift, against 71/82 and 78/82 for the objects where I could see something.

That looks like vindication. It is not, and the reason is in the selection:

class median measured SNR
STAR 49.5
QSO 8.5
BGS 5.0
LRG 3.8
ELG 1.3

All 18 flagged objects were ELG targets, and ELG is the faintest class in this cohort by a factor of three. "Faint and featureless" meant ELG here because of how the cohort was built, not because faint featureless spectra are ELGs. The same default failed in the previous round on a differently-composed sample.

So the honest statement is that the heuristic is a property of the sample, not of the spectra, and its success here is not evidence it will hold anywhere else. A rule that is right for a reason you cannot state is not yet knowledge — and this is the third time in this report that a comfortable result has turned out to rest on how the data were chosen rather than on what they contain.

What this test does establish, because the protocol was sealed and the selection Redrock-free:

  • the type can be read from an unlabelled spectrum at 98/100 against Redrock's own classification, essentially matching the imaging label's 99/100
  • letting that visual call choose the template family gives 95/100 redshifts within 1000 km/s, 95/97 against the rows Redrock itself trusts
  • the residual five-way gap is almost entirely BGS↔LRG, a boundary that exists in the targeting and not in the data
  • my only real weakness is the one this report identified two sections ago: a galaxy continuum that turns over can be mistaken for a star, and I still do not check for the Balmer series before deciding

32. The failures against a reference that vouches for itself¶

Of the five redshift failures, three carry ZWARN != 0 — Redrock does not trust its own answer there, so those are disagreements between two uncertain measurements rather than demonstrated errors. Filtering to ZWARN == 0 and the redshift wrong leaves two objects out of a hundred.

Nothing here re-examines an image to decide anything. The type calls were written to calls.json before the key was opened; this cell only reads what was recorded and joins it to the sealed answers. The spectra below are drawn purely to show where each call came from — the decision itself is already fixed on disk.

Blue marks the features my answer implies, dashed red where Redrock puts them. The red marks were not present during the blind read.

Two objects, and one mistake made twice. Both are low-redshift galaxies whose continuum rises and then turns over, and in both I took the turnover for a stellar continuum. In the zooms the blue marks — Ca II K, Mg b, Na D at rest, where a star would put them — sit on nothing, while Redrock's dashed 4000 Å break lands on the rise.

And the disproof is plainly visible in both. A strong emission spike sits exactly on Redrock's dashed H-alpha mark — 7580 Å in OBJ009, 7057 Å in OBJ078. Emission of that strength rules out a star outright, so the evidence against my call was not faint or subtle; it was sitting in the red half of a spectrum I never looked at, because I had already decided from the shape of the continuum in the blue.

That is a sharper lesson than the one I first wrote here. I described the missing step as "check the Balmer series before concluding star", which is true but too gentle. The real failure is that a call was made from one region and never tested against the rest of the spectrum. A turned-over continuum is not evidence of a star — a galaxy at z ≈ 0.1 has one too — and one glance at 6500-8000 Å would have settled it in either direction.

Everything else in the hundred either agrees with Redrock or disagrees only about which galaxy label to attach, and in all of those the redshift is right. Against the 97 rows Redrock vouches for, the method is 95/97.

Part V — A sealed blind test¶

33. Protocol, and the one thing changed since Part IV¶

50 fresh spectra — the 10 highest-SNR per class, none studied before (the seen list went 400 → 450). The protocol is identical to section 29: selection from TARGETID, SURVEY, PROGRAM, HEALPIX, COADD_FIBERSTATUS, DESI_TARGET and TSNR2_* only; SURVEY=="main", TARGETID>0, COADD_FIBERSTATUS==0; class by targeting bits with priority QSO > LRG > ELG > BGS_ANY > MWS_ANY; dedup on the highest TSNR2_<class> and never on ZCAT_PRIMARY / MAIN_PRIMARY, which rank by ZWARN; final cut on measured SNR; renders carrying an opaque id and nothing else, shuffled; and Z/ZWARN/SPECTYPE sealed at mode 600 until scoring.

The change is the order of operations for galaxies. Part IV read BGS or LRG off the picture and scored 13/20 on BGS. Section 32 traced that to a misconception: BGS versus LRG is not a spectral distinction, it is a redshift cut — worth 92.6% at z≈0.42 over 20,000 targets, against 75% by eye from the break edge. Judging it visually meant guessing a quantity the next step measures exactly.

So this time the image is only asked for STAR / QSO / ELG / GALAXY. For GALAXY the two galaxy families are fitted together and the BGS/LRG label is assigned afterwards from the fitted redshift. My recorded calls were STAR 10, QSO 10, ELG 10, GALAXY 20.

The star check that failed twice in Part IV was also applied: two objects here (OBJ006, OBJ035) show the rise-then-turnover continuum that produced both of those errors, and both were checked for emission in 6500–8000 Å before being called GALAXY rather than STAR.
